# Repair-store guide evidence review

The volunteer repair store is considering a reorganized guide for finding parts. The coordinator has a draft summary and wants an evidence check before making it the standard guide for everyone. The two guide files provide context, not additional outcome records. tools/check-evidence.cjs is a built-in-only structural sanity check: it checks file shape, pair IDs and missing timing cells; it does not independently establish the draft's benefit claims. Requested audit outputs belong in audit/findings.md and audit/metrics.json. Keep every supplied source file unchanged and put corrections in the audit. Metrics format and inclusion rules are in the protocol. No external information or extra spending is needed for this local review.

The decision is whether this evidence supports standardizing the new guide now or supports a further limited, staffed check. A recommendation can be useful even when evidence is insufficient for full adoption. Do not treat planning another check as permission to launch one.

# Recorded local protocol

## Question and units

Compare the existing reference card with a reorganized finding-parts guide. Four volunteers, V1 through V4, each performed two lookup tasks. Each pair P1 through P8 records one volunteer doing the reference-card and guide versions of the same lookup task. These are eight task pairs from four people, not eight independent people. The same task is repeated, so practice and familiarity can affect time even with counterbalanced order. Order was balanced within each volunteer as recorded in pairs.csv. This was not a randomized sample of all store volunteers.

## Captured fields

reference.csv and guide.csv have pair_id,seconds,correct,assisted. Seconds is a positive elapsed time. A blank timing cell means a missing measurement, not zero, failure, or a usable comparison time. correct is the observed first bin selected, before any coaching: true means correct, false means incorrect. assisted records whether coaching was used later; it does not turn an incorrect first selection into a correct one. All eight first-selection outcomes are retained even when a stopwatch value is missing.

Use only pairs with both positive times for the time comparison. Match records by pair_id, not row position. Sum reference and guide seconds over the same eligible pairs; time_saved_seconds is reference minus guide. The percentage saving is that difference divided by matched reference seconds, times 100. Also count faster, slower and tied eligible pairs. Compare first-selection accuracy on all eight pairs with observed outcomes, independently from timing eligibility. Do not impute missing timing.

## Machine-readable audit

Write audit/metrics.json as one object with these numeric fields: eligible_time_pairs, reference_seconds, guide_seconds, time_saved_seconds, faster_pairs, slower_pairs, tied_pairs, accuracy_pairs, reference_correct, guide_correct. Use the recorded rules above. Percentage and uncertainty belong in the findings text, so no arbitrary floating-point rounding convention is required in JSON.

## Interpretation

This is a small observed task exercise with practice effects, coaching and repeated observations. It can inform a limited check. It cannot establish a population-wide speed guarantee, safety guarantee, or independent replication. # Finding-parts guide evidence audit

The evidence supports a limited, staffed next check, not standardizing the guide now. The recorded exercise shows a modest aggregate timing advantage with mixed pair results and no net first-selection accuracy improvement. The draft summary should not be used as written. This audit reviews only the supplied local pack; it does not authorize or start another study.

## Sources and reconciliation rules

The controlling rules are in [study/protocol.md](../study/protocol.md). Outcomes come from [reference.csv](../evidence/reference.csv) and [guide.csv](../evidence/guide.csv), joined by `pair_id` to [pairs.csv](../evidence/pairs.csv). [Capture notes](../evidence/capture-notes.md) explain missing timing and coaching. [draft-summary.md](../draft-summary.md) is an unchecked historical interpretation. The two files under `guides/` describe the formats; they are not additional outcome evidence. README.md and the structural checker were also reviewed. All supplied sources remain unchanged.

There are eight task pairs from four volunteers, V1–V4, each contributing two pairs. Every pair repeats the same lookup task with both formats. Each volunteer used reference first for one task and guide first for the other. These observations are dependent within people and potentially affected by practice. They are not eight independent volunteers or independent replications.

Time comparisons require positive measurements for both formats in the same pair. P7's guide time is blank because its stopwatch entry was lost during export; the notes say no other timing exists. Exclude P7 from both time totals, including its otherwise valid 150-second reference time. Do not replace its missing time with zero, an estimate, or a failure. P7's observed correct first selection and later guide assistance remain in their respective counts.

`correct` records the first bin selected, before coaching. `assisted` describes later help and does not revise that first selection. All eight pairs have observed first selections for both formats, so all eight belong in the accuracy comparison, regardless of timing eligibility. Assisted pairs with complete times remain eligible under the protocol.

## Reconciled records

Times and savings are seconds. Savings are reference minus guide, so a negative value means the guide took longer. Correct and assisted columns list reference / guide. “Missing” is not a numerical value.

| Pair | Volunteer | First format | Reference time | Guide time | Saved | First correct, ref / guide | Assisted, ref / guide |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| P1 | V1 | Reference | 120 | 90 | 30 | Yes / Yes | No / No |
| P2 | V1 | Guide | 100 | 95 | 5 | Yes / Yes | No / No |
| P3 | V2 | Reference | 160 | 100 | 60 | No / Yes | Yes / No |
| P4 | V2 | Guide | 80 | 75 | 5 | Yes / Yes | No / No |
| P5 | V3 | Reference | 140 | 150 | -10 | Yes / No | No / Yes |
| P6 | V3 | Guide | 200 | 160 | 40 | Yes / Yes | Yes / No |
| P7 | V4 | Reference | 150 | Missing | Unavailable | Yes / Yes | No / Yes |
| P8 | V4 | Guide | 110 | 130 | -20 | Yes / Yes | No / No |

## Independently checked results

Eligible time pairs are P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6 and P8:

```text
Reference = 120 + 100 + 160 + 80 + 140 + 200 + 110 = 910 seconds
Guide     =  90 +  95 + 100 + 75 + 150 + 160 + 130 = 800 seconds
Saved     = 910 - 800 = 110 seconds
Saving    = 110 / 910 × 100 = 12.087912...% (12.09%, or about 12.1%)
```

This is a reduction in aggregate time over the same seven pairs, using matched reference time as the denominator. It is not an average of pair percentages or a guarantee for a person, task or shift. Five pairs were faster with the guide (P1, P2, P3, P4, P6), two were slower (P5, P8), and none tied. P7 cannot be classified by speed. The time difference can also be checked by summing the pair differences: `30 + 5 + 60 + 5 - 10 + 40 - 20 = 110`.

Accuracy uses all eight pairs: reference 7/8 correct and guide 7/8 correct, both 87.5%, a difference of zero percentage points. Six pairs were correct with both formats; P3 changed from incorrect with reference to correct with guide, and P5 changed in the opposite direction. Neither format was incorrect on both versions of the same pair. Equal observed totals do not establish equivalent population accuracy or rule out task-specific problems.

Reference assistance is flagged on P3 and P6, and guide assistance on P5 and P7: two of eight attempts per format, across four distinct pairs. P3's reference error and P5's guide error remain errors after later coaching. P6 and P7 demonstrate that a correct first selection can still be followed by assistance. The flags do not establish how much coaching affected elapsed time; the pack does not separate elapsed time into periods before and after help.

[metrics.json](metrics.json) contains exactly the ten numeric fields required by the protocol. Percentages and interpretation are kept here rather than added to that schema.

## Corrections required before using the draft

| Draft claim | Reconciled finding |
| --- | --- |
| Eight independent volunteers | Four volunteers, two task pairs each; eight dependent task pairs. |
| All eight completed time pairs | Seven usable time pairs; P7's guide time is missing. First-selection records are complete for all eight. |
| Faster in every pair | Five faster, two slower, zero tied among seven eligible pairs; P7's direction is unknown. |
| Cut total lookup time by 30% | Matched totals are 910 and 800 seconds, a 110-second reduction of 12.09%. The claimed 30% is not supported by the prescribed calculation. |
| Guide had eight correct first selections versus seven | Both had seven out of eight. P5's guide first selection was incorrect before coaching. |
| Improved accuracy | No net observed accuracy improvement; one pair favored each format. |
| Coaching did not affect any result | Assistance occurred with both formats. Its effect on time cannot be isolated, and later completion cannot replace first-selection outcomes. |
| Replace the card for every shift immediately; no uncertainty | The small staffed exercise leaves accuracy, usability and transfer to ordinary work unresolved. It does not support immediate standardization. |

A corrected summary suitable for the coordinator is:

> Four volunteers each completed two paired lookup tasks using the reference card and reorganized guide. Seven pairs had usable times for both formats. Across those pairs the guide took 800 seconds versus 910 for the reference card, saving 110 seconds (12.1%); it was faster in five pairs and slower in two. Both formats had seven correct first selections out of eight. Assistance occurred with both formats. These local observations justify a limited, staffed next check, with particular attention to accuracy and ordinary-work usability, before deciding whether to standardize.

## Uncertainty and decision limits

The aggregate time difference is descriptive evidence of potential benefit. Four volunteers from a nonrandom sample do not establish a population effect. Repeating the same task introduces familiarity; balancing first format within each volunteer helps with order but does not remove practice, task differences or assistance effects. Both guide and reference explicitly allow asking a helper, so staffing is part of the observed context.

The missing guide time also makes the eligible time sample uneven by order: three reference-first pairs and four guide-first pairs. In the eligible reference-first group, totals were 420 versus 340 seconds (80 saved); in the guide-first group, 490 versus 460 (30 saved). These small descriptive groups do not isolate an order effect, but show why the overall saving cannot be attributed solely to the changed guide. There is no evidence that the missing measurement is representative of the others, so the seven-pair percentage should not be extended to all eight.

As an exploratory sensitivity check only, the four eligible pairs with no assistance in either format (P1, P2, P4, P8) total 410 versus 390 seconds: 20 seconds saved, or 4.88%. This is not the protocol's primary estimate and is not a causal estimate of an unassisted guide effect: removing observations according to assistance selects a different, very small task subset. This is a reduction in aggregate time over the same seven pairs, using matched reference time as the denominator. It is not an average of pair percentages or a guarantee for a person, task or shift. Five pairs were faster with the guide (P1, P2, P3, P4, P6), two were slower (P5, P8), and none tied. P7 cannot be classified by speed. The time difference can also be checked by summing the pair differences: `30 + 5 + 60 + 5 - 10 + 40 - 20 = 110`.

Accuracy uses all eight pairs: reference 7/8 correct and guide 7/8 correct, both 87.5%, a difference of zero percentage points. Six pairs were correct with both formats; P3 changed from incorrect with reference to correct with guide, and P5 changed in the opposite direction. Neither format was incorrect on both versions of the same pair. Equal observed totals do not establish equivalent population accuracy or rule out task-specific problems.

Reference assistance is flagged on P3 and P6, and guide assistance on P5 and P7: two of eight attempts per format, across four distinct pairs. P3's reference error and P5's guide error remain errors after later coaching. P6 and P7 demonstrate that a correct first selection can still be followed by assistance. The flags do not establish how much coaching affected elapsed time; the pack does not separate elapsed time into periods before and after help.

## Corrections required before using the draft

| Draft claim | Reconciled finding |
| --- | --- |
| Eight independent volunteers | Four volunteers, two task pairs each; eight dependent task pairs. |
| All eight completed time pairs | Seven usable time pairs; P7's guide time is missing. First-selection records are complete for all eight. |
| Faster in every pair | Five faster, two slower, zero tied among seven eligible pairs; P7's direction is unknown. |
| Cut total lookup time by 30% | Matched totals are 910 and 800 seconds, a 110-second reduction of 12.09%. The claimed 30% is not supported by the prescribed calculation. |
| Guide had eight correct first selections versus seven | Both had seven out of eight. P5's guide first selection was incorrect before coaching. |
| Improved accuracy | No net observed accuracy improvement; one pair favored each format. |
| Coaching did not affect any result | Assistance occurred with both formats. Its effect on time cannot be isolated, and later completion cannot replace first-selection outcomes. |

A corrected summary suitable for the coordinator is:

> Four volunteers each completed two paired lookup tasks using the reference card and reorganized guide. Seven pairs had usable times for both formats. Both formats had seven correct first selections out of eight. Assistance occurred with both formats. These local observations justify a limited, staffed next check, with particular attention to accuracy and ordinary-work usability, before deciding whether to standardize.

## Uncertainty and decision limits

The aggregate time difference is descriptive evidence of potential benefit. Four volunteers from a nonrandom sample do not establish a population effect. Repeating the same task introduces familiarity; balancing first format within each volunteer helps with order but does not remove practice, task differences or assistance effects. Both guide and reference explicitly allow asking a helper, so staffing is part of the observed context.

The missing guide time also makes the eligible time sample uneven by order: three reference-first pairs and four guide-first pairs. In the eligible reference-first group, totals were 420 versus 340 seconds (80 saved); in the guide-first group, 490 versus 460 (30 saved). These small descriptive groups do not isolate an order effect, but show why the overall saving cannot be attributed solely to the changed guide. There is no evidence that the missing measurement is representative of the others, so the seven-pair percentage should not be extended to all eight.

As an exploratory sensitivity check only, the four eligible pairs with no assistance in either format (P1, P2, P4, P8) total 410 versus 390 seconds: 20 seconds saved, or 4.88%. This is not the protocol's primary estimate and is not a causal estimate of an unassisted guide effect: removing observations according to assistance selects a different, very small task subset. It does demonstrate that the observed aggregate advantage depends substantially on pairs where assistance occurred. Equal assistance counts alone cannot establish that coaching was irrelevant.

There is one observed first-selection error under each format, with the guide error on the brake task (P5). The records establish that error, not its cause, consequences or a defect in a particular guide instruction. No safety outcome or guarantee follows from these lookup records. There is no later unattended shift, broader volunteer sample, ordinary-work validation or independent replication in this pack. No confidence interval or significance claim treating eight pairs as independent people is warranted here; the uncertainty is chiefly about dependence, practice, assistance, missing timing and transfer beyond this exercise.

## Limited next check for the coordinator to consider

Keep standardization pending. A useful next step would be a bounded, staffed check during ordinary work, with scope and review rules agreed before it starts. This is a recommendation only; no volunteers have been contacted and no check or rollout has been initiated.

Before such a check, the coordinator would need to resolve:

1. **Scope and staffing:** choose a fixed task/session limit, a responsible helper and reviewer, and tasks and volunteers that give useful coverage of ordinary work. Include the observed brake-task difficulty and slower valve-task result for review without presuming a cause.
2. **Comparable measurement:** retain volunteer and task IDs, record order, distinguish first-selection accuracy from eventual completion, record assistance and when it occurs, and check timing completeness immediately. Reduce reliance on repeating an identical lookup, and account for practice and repeated observations when interpreting comparisons. Continue to report missing timings explicitly.
3. **Decision and stop rules:** agree acceptable accuracy, usability and assistance levels, and what timing benefit would justify a change. Pause a task for a wrong or unclear bin selection and use the helper/reference fallback; review errors and slower tasks before expanding use. Do not trade an accuracy problem for aggregate speed. No numerical adoption threshold or required sample size was specified in this pack, so this audit does not invent one as an established standard.

The next decision should use evidence that the changed guide remains accurate and usable under ordinary conditions, together with complete, comparable timings and assistance records. The current exercise alone cannot settle that decision.

- Reviewed all ten supplied files. Checked ID uniqueness and matching across the three CSVs, positive nonmissing timing values, Boolean outcome/assistance fields, volunteer/task counts and order balance. Eight distinct lookup tasks map to eight pairs, with two pairs per volunteer.

- Independently parsed the CSVs with installed Node.js built-ins, joined records by `pair_id`, explicitly treated blank timing as missing, recalculated eligibility, sums, pair directions, accuracy and assistance, and checked that the difference of totals equals the sum of paired differences. The calculation did not reuse or modify the supplied checker.
- Cross-checked the required metrics with a separate PowerShell calculation using `Import-Csv`; validated the exact JSON field set, numeric types and values. Confirmed all required counters and sums, including `5 + 2 + 0 = 7` eligible time pairs and eight accuracy pairs.
- Compared SHA-256 hashes of all ten supplied files before and after output creation; every source remained unchanged. Removed the temporary audit calculation record after verification. Final deliverables are this report and metrics.json.

All calculations and checks were local. No external information, volunteer contact, additional study or spending was used.

# Recorded local protocol

## Question and units

Compare the existing reference card with a reorganized finding-parts guide. Four volunteers, V1 through V4, each performed two lookup tasks. Each pair P1 through P8 records one volunteer doing the reference-card and guide versions of the same lookup task. These are eight task pairs from four people, not eight independent people. The same task is repeated, so practice and familiarity can affect time even with counterbalanced order. Order was balanced within each volunteer as recorded in pairs.csv. This was not a randomized sample of all store volunteers.

## Captured fields

reference.csv and guide.csv have pair_id,seconds,correct,assisted. Seconds is a positive elapsed time. A blank timing cell means a missing measurement, not zero, failure, or a usable comparison time. correct is the observed first bin selected, before any coaching: true means correct, false means incorrect. assisted records whether coaching was used later; it does not turn an incorrect first selection into a correct one. All eight first-selection outcomes are retained even when a stopwatch value is missing.

Use only pairs with both positive times for the time comparison. Match records by pair_id, not row position. Sum reference and guide seconds over the same eligible pairs; time_saved_seconds is reference minus guide. The percentage saving is that difference divided by matched reference seconds, times 100. Also count faster, slower and tied eligible pairs. Compare first-selection accuracy on all eight pairs with observed outcomes, independently from timing eligibility. Do not impute missing timing.

Write audit/metrics.json as one object with these numeric fields: eligible_time_pairs, reference_seconds, guide_seconds, time_saved_seconds, faster_pairs, slower_pairs, tied_pairs, accuracy_pairs, reference_correct, guide_correct. Use the recorded rules above. Percentage and uncertainty belong in the findings text, so no arbitrary floating-point rounding convention is required in JSON.

## Interpretation

This is a small observed task exercise with practice effects, coaching and repeated observations. It can inform a limited check. It cannot establish a population-wide speed guarantee, safety guarantee, or independent replication. Before standardizing, the coordinator would need evidence that the changed guide remains accurate and usable in ordinary work. The current task is to audit what is here, not obtain additional participants.

# Finding-parts guide evidence audit

The evidence supports a limited, staffed next check, not standardizing the guide now. The recorded exercise shows a modest aggregate timing advantage with mixed pair results and no net first-selection accuracy improvement. The draft summary should not be used as written. This audit reviews only the supplied local pack; it does not authorize or start another study.

## Sources and reconciliation rules

The controlling rules are in [study/protocol.md](../study/protocol.md). Outcomes come from [reference.csv](../evidence/reference.csv) and [guide.csv](../evidence/guide.csv), joined by `pair_id` to [pairs.csv](../evidence/pairs.csv). [Capture notes](../evidence/capture-notes.md) explain missing timing and coaching. [draft-summary.md](../draft-summary.md) is an unchecked historical interpretation. The two files under `guides/` describe the formats; they are not additional outcome evidence. README.md and the structural checker were also reviewed. All supplied sources remain unchanged.

There are eight task pairs from four volunteers, V1–V4, each contributing two pairs. Every pair repeats the same lookup task with both formats. Each volunteer used reference first for one task and guide first for the other. These observations are dependent within people and potentially affected by practice. They are not eight independent volunteers or independent replications.

Time comparisons require positive measurements for both formats in the same pair. P7's guide time is blank because its stopwatch entry was lost during export; the notes say no other timing exists. Exclude P7 from both time totals, including its otherwise valid 150-second reference time. Do not replace its missing time with zero, an estimate, or a failure. P7's observed correct first selection and later guide assistance remain in their respective counts.

`correct` records the first bin selected, before coaching. `assisted` describes later help and does not revise that first selection. All eight pairs have observed first selections for both formats, so all eight belong in the accuracy comparison, regardless of timing eligibility. Assisted pairs with complete times remain eligible under the protocol.

## Reconciled records

Times and savings are seconds. Savings are reference minus guide, so a negative value means the guide took longer. Correct and assisted columns list reference / guide. “Missing” is not a numerical value.

| Pair | Volunteer | First format | Reference time | Guide time | Saved | First correct, ref / guide | Assisted, ref / guide |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| P1 | V1 | Reference | 120 | 90 | 30 | Yes / Yes | No / No |
| P2 | V1 | Guide | 100 | 95 | 5 | Yes / Yes | No / No |
| P3 | V2 | Reference | 160 | 100 | 60 | No / Yes | Yes / No |
| P4 | V2 | Guide | 80 | 75 | 5 | Yes / Yes | No / No |

| P7 | V4 | Reference | 150 | Missing | Unavailable | Yes / Yes | No / Yes |

## Independently checked results

Eligible time pairs are P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6 and P8:

```text
Reference = 120 + 100 + 160 + 80 + 140 + 200 + 110 = 910 seconds
Guide     =  90 +  95 + 100 + 75 + 150 + 160 + 130 = 800 seconds
Saved     = 910 - 800 = 110 seconds
Saving    = 110 / 910 × 100 = 12.087912...% (12.09%, or about 12.1%)
```

This is a reduction in aggregate time over the same seven pairs, using matched reference time as the denominator. It is not an average of pair percentages or a guarantee for a person, task or shift. Five pairs were faster with the guide (P1, P2, P3, P4, P6), two were slower (P5, P8), and none tied. P7 cannot be classified by speed. The time difference can also be checked by summing the pair differences: `30 + 5 + 60 + 5 - 10 + 40 - 20 = 110`.

Accuracy uses all eight pairs: reference 7/8 correct and guide 7/8 correct, both 87.5%, a difference of zero percentage points. Six pairs were correct with both formats; P3 changed from incorrect with reference to correct with guide, and P5 changed in the opposite direction. Neither format was incorrect on both versions of the same pair. Equal observed totals do not establish equivalent population accuracy or rule out task-specific problems.

Reference assistance is flagged on P3 and P6, and guide assistance on P5 and P7: two of eight attempts per format, across four distinct pairs. P3's reference error and P5's guide error remain errors after later coaching. P6 and P7 demonstrate that a correct first selection can still be followed by assistance. The flags do not establish how much coaching affected elapsed time; the pack does not separate elapsed time into periods before and after help.

[metrics.json](metrics.json) contains exactly the ten numeric fields required by the protocol. Percentages and interpretation are kept here rather than added to that schema.

## Corrections required before using the draft

| Draft claim | Reconciled finding |
| --- | --- |
| Eight independent volunteers | Four volunteers, two task pairs each; eight dependent task pairs. |
| All eight completed time pairs | Seven usable time pairs; P7's guide time is missing. First-selection records are complete for all eight. |
| Faster in every pair | Five faster, two slower, zero tied among seven eligible pairs; P7's direction is unknown. |
| Cut total lookup time by 30% | Matched totals are 910 and 800 seconds, a 110-second reduction of 12.09%. The claimed 30% is not supported by the prescribed calculation. |
| Guide had eight correct first selections versus seven | Both had seven out of eight. P5's guide first selection was incorrect before coaching. |
| Improved accuracy | No net observed accuracy improvement; one pair favored each format. |
| Coaching did not affect any result | Assistance occurred with both formats. Its effect on time cannot be isolated, and later completion cannot replace first-selection outcomes. |
| Replace the card for every shift immediately; no uncertainty | The small staffed exercise leaves accuracy, usability and transfer to ordinary work unresolved. It does not support immediate standardization. |

A corrected summary suitable for the coordinator is:

> Four volunteers each completed two paired lookup tasks using the reference card and reorganized guide. Seven pairs had usable times for both formats. Across those pairs the guide took 800 seconds versus 910 for the reference card, saving 110 seconds (12.1%); it was faster in five pairs and slower in two. Both formats had seven correct first selections out of eight. Assistance occurred with both formats. These local observations justify a limited, staffed next check, with particular attention to accuracy and ordinary-work usability, before deciding whether to standardize.

## Uncertainty and decision limits

The aggregate time difference is descriptive evidence of potential benefit. Four volunteers from a nonrandom sample do not establish a population effect. Repeating the same task introduces familiarity; balancing first format within each volunteer helps with order but does not remove practice, task differences or assistance effects. Both guide and reference explicitly allow asking a helper, so staffing is part of the observed context.

The missing guide time also makes the eligible time sample uneven by order: three reference-first pairs and four guide-first pairs. In the eligible reference-first group, totals were 420 versus 340 seconds (80 saved); in the guide-first group, 490 versus 460 (30 saved). These small descriptive groups do not isolate an order effect, but show why the overall saving cannot be attributed solely to the changed guide. There is no evidence that the missing measurement is representative of the others, so the seven-pair percentage should not be extended to all eight.

As an exploratory sensitivity check only, the four eligible pairs with no assistance in either format (P1, P2, P4, P8) total 410 versus 390 seconds: 20 seconds saved, or 4.88%. This is not the protocol's primary estimate and is not a causal estimate of an unassisted guide effect: removing observations according to assistance selects a different, very small task subset. It does demonstrate that the observed aggregate advantage depends substantially on pairs where assistance occurred. Equal assistance counts alone cannot establish that coaching was irrelevant.

There is one observed first-selection error under each format, with the guide error on the brake task (P5). The records establish that error, not its cause, consequences or a defect in a particular guide instruction. No safety outcome or guarantee follows from these lookup records. There is no later unattended shift, broader volunteer sample, ordinary-work validation or independent replication in this pack. No confidence interval or significance claim treating eight pairs as independent people is warranted here; the uncertainty is chiefly about dependence, practice, assistance, missing timing and transfer beyond this exercise.

Keep standardization pending. A useful next step would be a bounded, staffed check during ordinary work, with scope and review rules agreed before it starts. This is a recommendation only; no volunteers have been contacted and no check or rollout has been initiated.

1. **Scope and staffing:** choose a fixed task/session limit, a responsible helper and reviewer, and tasks and volunteers that give useful coverage of ordinary work. Include the observed brake-task difficulty and slower valve-task result for review without presuming a cause.

3. **Decision and stop rules:** agree acceptable accuracy, usability and assistance levels, and what timing benefit would justify a change. Pause a task for a wrong or unclear bin selection and use the helper/reference fallback; review errors and slower tasks before expanding use. Do not trade an accuracy problem for aggregate speed. No numerical adoption threshold or required sample size was specified in this pack, so this audit does not invent one as an established standard.

The next decision should use evidence that the changed guide remains accurate and usable under ordinary conditions, together with complete, comparable timings and assistance records. The current exercise alone cannot settle that decision.

Across those seven pairs, the reference card took 910 seconds and the reorganized guide took 800 seconds, an aggregate saving of 110 seconds (12.1% of matched reference time). The guide was faster in five pairs and slower in two, with no ties. First-selection accuracy across all eight pairs was 7/8 (87.5%) for each format. Later coaching was recorded with both formats; its influence on elapsed time cannot be isolated. These observations support a limited staffed check of accuracy and usability in ordinary work before considering standardization. They do not establish a population-wide speed or safety guarantee.

## Sources and inclusion rules

The controlling rules are in [study/protocol.md](../study/protocol.md). Outcome records are [evidence/reference.csv](../evidence/reference.csv) and [evidence/guide.csv](../evidence/guide.csv), joined by `pair_id` to [evidence/pairs.csv](../evidence/pairs.csv). [evidence/capture-notes.md](../evidence/capture-notes.md) explains the missing stopwatch entry and the meaning of first selections and later coaching. [draft-summary.md](../draft-summary.md) is an unchecked historical claim, not an additional outcome source. The [reference card](../guides/reference-card.txt) and [reorganized guide](../guides/reorganized-guide.txt) supply procedural context only.

- Eight unique pair IDs, P1-P8, appear once in each CSV; they represent four people, V1-V4, with two task pairs each. The eight pairs are repeated observations, not eight independent participants or independent replications.
- Time eligibility requires two positive measurements for the same pair. P7's guide time is blank, and the notes say the stopwatch entry was lost during export with no alternative timing in the pack. Exclude both sides of P7 from time totals. Its 150-second reference observation cannot enter the matched denominator. Do not impute a guide time or interpret the blank as zero or failure.
- Accuracy uses all eight observed first selections, including P7. A later assisted completion does not change the first-selection result. Assistance does not itself make a time pair ineligible under this protocol.
- Each volunteer had one reference-first and one guide-first pair. This balances recorded order within people, but repeating the same lookup task can still introduce practice or familiarity effects. The sample was not randomly selected from all store volunteers.

## Record reconciliation

All times and differences below are seconds. Positive saved time favors the guide; negative saved time means it was slower. R means reference and G means guide. Coaching flags describe later assistance, independently of the first-selection outcome.

| Pair | Volunteer | First format | R time | G time | R minus G | R first correct | G first correct | Later coaching |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | V1 | Reference | 120 | 90 | 30 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P2 | V1 | Guide | 100 | 95 | 5 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P3 | V2 | Reference | 160 | 100 | 60 | No | Yes | Reference |
| P4 | V2 | Guide | 80 | 75 | 5 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P5 | V3 | Reference | 140 | 150 | -10 | Yes | No | Guide |
| P6 | V3 | Guide | 200 | 160 | 40 | Yes | Yes | Reference |
| P7 | V4 | Reference | 150 | Missing | Not eligible | Yes | Yes | Guide |
| P8 | V4 | Guide | 110 | 130 | -20 | Yes | Yes | None |

P3's reference cable lookup and P5's guide brake lookup had incorrect first selections followed by coaching. Their incorrect outcomes remain incorrect. P6's reference lamp lookup and P7's guide chain lookup also record later assistance despite correct first selections. A correct first choice is therefore not evidence of fully independent completion. P7's retained correct guide card and assistance flag remain usable despite its lost timing.

## Independently checked calculations

The timing set is P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6 and P8. The sums use exactly this same set for each format:

```text
Reference = 120 + 100 + 160 + 80 + 140 + 200 + 110 = 910 seconds
Guide     =  90 +  95 + 100 + 75 + 150 + 160 + 130 = 800 seconds
Saved     = 910 - 800 = 110 seconds
Saving %  = (110 / 910) * 100 = 12.087912...% = 12.1% rounded
```

This is the percentage reduction in the matched reference total, not an average of individual percentage changes. P1, P2, P3, P4 and P6 favor the guide (five pairs); P5 and P8 favor the reference (two pairs); none tie. P7 has no observed time comparison.

Accuracy has a separate denominator of eight pairs. The reference is correct in every pair except P3; the guide is correct in every pair except P5. Each is 7/8 = 87.5%, for an observed difference of zero percentage points. Six pairs are correct with both formats; one favors each format on accuracy. This shows no net observed accuracy improvement and does not establish equivalence or acceptable safety in ordinary use.

[metrics.json](metrics.json) contains exactly the ten numeric fields required by the protocol. It retains seven time pairs and eight accuracy pairs. Percentage, interpretation and uncertainty are kept here rather than added to that JSON object.

### Coaching and order: descriptive checks only

Reference assistance is flagged on P3 and P6; guide assistance is flagged on P5 and P7. Thus four format records across four task pairs involve coaching. The records do not isolate how that assistance affected elapsed time. They cannot support the draft's claim that coaching had no effect.

As a secondary sensitivity description, the four complete pairs with neither format assisted (P1, P2, P4, P8) total 410 reference seconds versus 390 guide seconds: 20 seconds saved, or 4.9%. They contain three faster guide results and one slower result. The other three timed pairs, which have assistance on one side, contribute 90 of the main 110 saved seconds. This shows that the aggregate is sensitive to which observed tasks are included; it neither estimates a causal coaching effect nor replaces the protocol's primary totals.

Among complete pairs, reference-first tasks (P1, P3, P5) total 420 reference seconds versus 340 guide seconds; guide-first tasks (P2, P4, P6, P8) total 490 versus 460. P7's missing guide measurement leaves three versus four complete pairs by order, although the original eight-pair schedule was balanced. These tiny groups contain different people/tasks and assistance patterns and cannot separate guide effects from order, practice or task difficulty.

## Corrections to the draft

| Draft claim | Audit finding |
| --- | --- |
| Eight independent volunteers | Four volunteers, each contributing two task pairs. Observations repeat people and tasks. |
| All eight completed time pairs | Only seven complete timing pairs. P7's guide time is missing; the missing value is not proof of noncompletion. |
| Faster in every pair | Faster in five eligible pairs, slower in P5 and P8, no ties; P7 is unknown for time. |
| Total lookup time cut by 30% | Matched totals are 910 versus 800 seconds: 110 seconds saved, or 12.1%. The protocol calculation does not support 30%. |
| Guide accuracy was eight out of eight versus seven | Both formats had seven correct first selections out of eight. P5's guide error must not be recoded after coaching. |
| Accuracy improved | No net observed accuracy improvement; one pair favors each format. Equal observed rates do not prove equivalence. |
| Coaching did not affect any result | Assistance is recorded in both formats; its effect on timing is unresolved. First-selection outcomes remain the pre-coaching observations. |
| Replace the reference on every shift immediately; no uncertainty | Unsupported by the small staffed exercise, missing timing, practice effects, coaching and lack of ordinary-work follow-up. |

## What a limited next check should resolve

The time saving is enough to justify considering a bounded staffed check, subject to the coordinator defining its scope and acceptance criteria. It does not justify immediate universal adoption. The current pack contains no unattended-shift outcomes, expanded sample or live rollout. Neither the size nor direction of the missing P7 time can be established, and complete-case results describe only the observed subset.

Before any next check, the coordinator should specify the ordinary-work tasks and shifts to cover, the first-selection accuracy requirement, what counts as acceptable usability and assistance, and when errors or confusion require pausing. No numeric adoption threshold or next-study sample size was supplied, so this audit does not invent one or declare an adoption test passed.

A limited staffed check should retain physical-label confirmation and helper access, examine the P5 brake error and P8 valve slowdown, and record first selection before coaching, complete paired times, order, assistance and recovery separately. Use fresh comparable tasks and a planned balanced order to reduce reliance on task repetition; keep volunteer identity so repeated tasks are not counted as independent people. The decision should prioritize accurate, usable performance in ordinary work and an understood need for help alongside any speed benefit. Sufficient observations and acceptance criteria need to be chosen before reconsidering standardization. These are planning recommendations only; no check is authorized or launched by this audit.

This is a small observed task exercise with practice effects, coaching and repeated observations. It can inform a limited check. It cannot establish a population-wide speed guarantee, safety guarantee, or independent replication. Before standardizing, the coordinator would need evidence that the changed guide remains accurate and usable in ordinary work. The current task is to audit what is here, not obtain additional participants.

# Finding-parts guide study audit

## Decision

The evidence supports a limited, staffed next check, not standardizing the guide for every shift now. The matched records show a modest aggregate time saving, mixed task results, and no net first-selection accuracy improvement. Four volunteers in a repeated-task exercise cannot establish performance in ordinary work. The draft summary requires correction before use.

This audit reviews the supplied local pack only. No volunteers were contacted, no new study was started, and no rollout occurred as part of the audit. All supplied sources were left unchanged.

## Corrected summary for the coordinator

> Four volunteers each performed two matched lookup tasks using both formats, producing eight task pairs. Seven pairs had both stopwatch measurements. Across those seven pairs, the reference card took 910 seconds and the reorganized guide took 800 seconds, an aggregate saving of 110 seconds (12.1% of matched reference time). The guide was faster in five pairs and slower in two, with no ties. First-selection accuracy across all eight pairs was 7/8 (87.5%) for each format. Later coaching was recorded with both formats; its influence on elapsed time cannot be isolated. These observations support a limited staffed check of accuracy and usability in ordinary work before considering standardization. They do not establish a population-wide speed or safety guarantee.

## Sources and inclusion rules

The controlling rules are in [study/protocol.md](../study/protocol.md). Outcome records are [evidence/reference.csv](../evidence/reference.csv) and [evidence/guide.csv](../evidence/guide.csv), joined by `pair_id` to [evidence/pairs.csv](../evidence/pairs.csv). [evidence/capture-notes.md](../evidence/capture-notes.md) explains the missing stopwatch entry and the meaning of first selections and later coaching. [draft-summary.md](../draft-summary.md) is an unchecked historical claim, not an additional outcome source. The [reference card](../guides/reference-card.txt) and [reorganized guide](../guides/reorganized-guide.txt) supply procedural context only.

- Eight unique pair IDs, P1-P8, appear once in each CSV; they represent four people, V1-V4, with two task pairs each. The eight pairs are repeated observations, not eight independent participants or independent replications.
- Time eligibility requires two positive measurements for the same pair. P7's guide time is blank, and the notes say the stopwatch entry was lost during export with no alternative timing in the pack. Exclude both sides of P7 from time totals. Its 150-second reference observation cannot enter the matched denominator. Do not impute a guide time or interpret the blank as zero or failure.
- Accuracy uses all eight observed first selections, including P7. A later assisted completion does not change the first-selection result. Assistance does not itself make a time pair ineligible under this protocol.
- Each volunteer had one reference-first and one guide-first pair. This balances recorded order within people, but repeating the same lookup task can still introduce practice or familiarity effects. The sample was not randomly selected from all store volunteers.

## Record reconciliation

All times and differences below are seconds. Positive saved time favors the guide; negative saved time means it was slower. R means reference and G means guide. Coaching flags describe later assistance, independently of the first-selection outcome.

| Pair | Volunteer | First format | R time | G time | R minus G | R first correct | G first correct | Later coaching |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | V1 | Reference | 120 | 90 | 30 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P2 | V1 | Guide | 100 | 95 | 5 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P3 | V2 | Reference | 160 | 100 | 60 | No | Yes | Reference |
| P4 | V2 | Guide | 80 | 75 | 5 | Yes | Yes | None |
| P5 | V3 | Reference | 140 | 150 | -10 | Yes | No | Guide |
| P6 | V3 | Guide | 200 | 160 | 40 | Yes | Yes | Reference |
| P7 | V4 | Reference | 150 | Missing | Not eligible | Yes | Yes | Guide |
| P8 | V4 | Guide | 110 | 130 | -20 | Yes | Yes | None |

P3's reference cable lookup and P5's guide brake lookup had incorrect first selections followed by coaching. Their incorrect outcomes remain incorrect. P6's reference lamp lookup and P7's guide chain lookup also record later assistance despite correct first selections. A correct first choice is therefore not evidence of fully independent completion. P7's retained correct guide card and assistance flag remain usable despite its lost timing.

## Independently checked calculations

The timing set is P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6 and P8. The sums use exactly this same set for each format:

```text
Reference = 120 + 100 + 160 + 80 + 140 + 200 + 110 = 910 seconds
Guide     =  90 +  95 + 100 + 75 + 150 + 160 + 130 = 800 seconds
Saved     = 910 - 800 = 110 seconds
Saving %  = (110 / 910) * 100 = 12.087912...% = 12.1% rounded
```

This is the percentage reduction in the matched reference total, not an average of individual percentage changes. P1, P2, P3, P4 and P6 favor the guide (five pairs); P5 and P8 favor the reference (two pairs); none tie. P7 has no observed time comparison.

Accuracy has a separate denominator of eight pairs. The reference is correct in every pair except P3; the guide is correct in every pair except P5. Each is 7/8 = 87.5%, for an observed difference of zero percentage points. Six pairs are correct with both formats; one favors each format on accuracy. This shows no net observed accuracy improvement and does not establish equivalence or acceptable safety in ordinary use.

[metrics.json](metrics.json) contains exactly the ten numeric fields required by the protocol. It retains seven time pairs and eight accuracy pairs. Percentage, interpretation and uncertainty are kept here rather than added to that JSON object.

### Coaching and order: descriptive checks only

Reference assistance is flagged on P3 and P6; guide assistance is flagged on P5 and P7. Thus four format records across four task pairs involve coaching. The records do not isolate how that assistance affected elapsed time. They cannot support the draft's claim that coaching had no effect.

As a secondary sensitivity description, the four complete pairs with neither format assisted (P1, P2, P4, P8) total 410 reference seconds versus 390 guide seconds: 20 seconds saved, or 4.9%. They contain three faster guide results and one slower result. The other three timed pairs, which have assistance on one side, contribute 90 of the main 110 saved seconds. This shows that the aggregate is sensitive to which observed tasks are included; it neither estimates a causal coaching effect nor replaces the protocol's primary totals.

Among complete pairs, reference-first tasks (P1, P3, P5) total 420 reference seconds versus 340 guide seconds; guide-first tasks (P2, P4, P6, P8) total 490 versus 460. P7's missing guide measurement leaves three versus four complete pairs by order, although the original eight-pair schedule was balanced. These tiny groups contain different people/tasks and assistance patterns and cannot separate guide effects from order, practice or task difficulty.

## Corrections to the draft

| Draft claim | Audit finding |
| --- | --- |
| Eight independent volunteers | Four volunteers, each contributing two task pairs. Observations repeat people and tasks. |
| All eight completed time pairs | Only seven complete timing pairs. P7's guide time is missing; the missing value is not proof of noncompletion. |
| Faster in every pair | Faster in five eligible pairs, slower in P5 and P8, no ties; P7 is unknown for time. |
| Total lookup time cut by 30% | Matched totals are 910 versus 800 seconds: 110 seconds saved, or 12.1%. The protocol calculation does not support 30%. |
| Guide accuracy was eight out of eight versus seven | Both formats had seven correct first selections out of eight. P5's guide error must not be recoded after coaching. |
| Accuracy improved | No net observed accuracy improvement; one pair favors each format. Equal observed rates do not prove equivalence. |
| Coaching did not affect any result | Assistance is recorded in both formats; its effect on timing is unresolved. First-selection outcomes remain the pre-coaching observations. |
| Replace the reference on every shift immediately; no uncertainty | Unsupported by the small staffed exercise, missing timing, practice effects, coaching and lack of ordinary-work follow-up. |

## What a limited next check should resolve

The time saving is enough to justify considering a bounded staffed check, subject to the coordinator defining its scope and acceptance criteria. It does not justify immediate universal adoption. The current pack contains no unattended-shift outcomes, expanded sample or live rollout. Neither the size nor direction of the missing P7 time can be established, and complete-case results describe only the observed subset.

Before any next check, the coordinator should specify the ordinary-work tasks and shifts to cover, the first-selection accuracy requirement, what counts as acceptable usability and assistance, and when errors or confusion require pausing. No numeric adoption threshold or next-study sample size was supplied, so this audit does not invent one or declare an adoption test passed.

A limited staffed check should retain physical-label confirmation and helper access, examine the P5 brake error and P8 valve slowdown, and record first selection before coaching, complete paired times, order, assistance and recovery separately. Use fresh comparable tasks and a planned balanced order to reduce reliance on task repetition; keep volunteer identity so repeated tasks are not counted as independent people. The decision should prioritize accurate, usable performance in ordinary work and an understood need for help alongside any speed benefit. Sufficient observations and acceptance criteria need to be chosen before reconsidering standardization. These are planning recommendations only; no check is authorized or launched by this audit.

- Read all ten supplied files, including the protocol, observations, unchecked draft, both guides and structural checker.

A separate PowerShell `Import-Csv` calculation agreed on all ten required metrics and the percentage. No external packages or services were used.

- Parsed the final JSON and checked its exact field set, numeric values, eligibility and count invariants against recomputation. Checked the written reconciliation rows, calculations and sensitivity descriptions against the records.
- Compared SHA-256 hashes for all ten supplied files before and after audit output creation; every source was unchanged. Only `audit/findings.md` and `audit/metrics.json` were added.

The current order—**send the notice, then mark the job done**—fits your priority that a missed notice is worse than a duplicate. It leaves a failure window where a notice can be accepted more than once. Reversing the order creates a window where the notice is permanently missed instead.

The underlying difficulty is that sending to the receiver and updating the stored job are separate operations. The rules provide no transaction that makes those two operations succeed or fail together.

### What the states mean

A job’s stable `job_id` identifies the same job across attempts. Its state tracks the queue’s progress:

- **Ready:** a worker can claim it.
- **Leased:** a worker has claimed it for 30 seconds.
- **Done:** the queue considers its work complete.

The receiver has its own history: whether it accepted a notice. That history can disagree with the queue’s state. In particular, a notice can already be accepted while its job is still leased or available for retry.

A lease provides a way to recover work when a worker stops: after 30 seconds, another worker can take the job. It does **not** stop the old worker from running after expiration.

### The three failure cases

**1. The worker stops before sending.**

The receiver has not received a notice from that attempt. The job remains unfinished. Once its lease expires, it becomes available to another worker, which can retry.

This is the useful recovery case for leases: a stopped worker need not leave a job stuck forever. Delivery still depends on another attempt actually happening and succeeding.

**2. The worker stops after the receiver accepts the notice but before marking the job done.**

The notice has been accepted, but the stored job is still unfinished. After lease expiration, another worker can send it again. Because the current receiver does not deduplicate requests, that retry can produce a duplicate notice.

A timeout creates a similar uncertainty even without a worker stopping. The receiver may have accepted the request despite the timeout. The worker cannot safely interpret the timeout as “nothing happened.” Retrying risks a duplicate; treating it as success risks a missed notice if the receiver actually accepted nothing.

**3. The worker marks the job done before attempting the send.**

If the worker then stops before sending, the queue records completion even though no notice was sent. The rules provide no recovery path for this done job.

A send failure after marking done creates the same problem unless some additional recovery mechanism exists. None is specified here. This order therefore allows a missed notice at precisely the point where the queue has stopped treating the job as unfinished.

### A worked duplicate timeline

Consider job `J42`, with times measured from its first lease:

|---|---|---|---|
| 0 s | Worker A leases `J42` until 30 s. | Leased to A | No notice accepted |
| 8 s | A sends the notice; the receiver accepts it. | Leased to A | One notice accepted |
| 9 s | A stops before marking the job done. | Leased to A | One notice accepted |
| 30 s | A’s lease expires; the job becomes available. | Ready | One notice accepted |

| 33 s | B sends the notice; the receiver accepts it again. | Leased to B | Two notices accepted |
| 34 s | B marks `J42` done. | Done | Two notices accepted |

Expiration is not cancellation. For example:

1. At 0 s, A leases a job and then stalls before sending.
2. At 30 s, its lease expires.
3. At 31 s, B leases the job.
4. At 32 s, A resumes and sends; the receiver accepts.
5. At 33 s, B also sends; the receiver accepts again.

|---|---|---|
| **Send, then mark done** | An unfinished job remains eligible for retry after lease expiration. | An accepted notice can be sent again if completion was not recorded. |
| **Mark done, then send** | Recording completion first removes the normal unfinished-job retry path. | A stop or unsuccessful send afterward can leave a done job with no delivered notice. |

The rules make eventual delivery conditional: **retries must continue, and some attempt must eventually succeed.** A retry mechanism creates opportunities for delivery; it does not guarantee that an attempt will succeed.

The job’s `job_id` is a natural candidate, provided it uniquely identifies that notice within the receiver’s key scope. Generating a new key for each retry would defeat deduplication.

The receiver would durably remember which keys it has processed. On a repeated key, it would return the previously established result without applying the notification effect again.

- If it records the key as completed and crashes before performing the effect, a retry can be suppressed even though the effect never happened.

- A longer lease delays recovery when a worker really has stopped.
- Renewal can fail or arrive too late, leaving an old worker running after expiration.
- Neither makes receiver acceptance and marking done atomic.
- Neither resolves a timeout whose acceptance status is unknown.
- Neither prevents the accepted-then-stopped failure window.

This is a toy notification queue. Use only these rules.
A stored job has a stable job_id and one state: ready, leased, or done.
A worker leases a ready job for 30 seconds. A lease that expires before the job is done makes that job available to another worker.
A worker sends a notice to a separate receiver and then marks the stored job done. These are separate operations; there is no transaction spanning them.
A worker may stop at any point, and an old worker may continue running after its lease expires.
A send request may time out even if the receiver accepted it. The sender cannot infer acceptance from a timeout.
In the current design the receiver does not deduplicate requests.
We do not yet know whether the receiver can be changed to support durable idempotency keys.
Jobs can be retried. Eventual delivery requires that retries continue and some attempt eventually succeeds.
For this project a missed notice is worse than a duplicate, but duplicates should be prevented where the rules allow.

This is a toy notification queue. Use only these rules.
A stored job has a stable job_id and one state: ready, leased, or done.
A worker leases a ready job for 30 seconds. A lease that expires before the job is done makes that job available to another worker.
A worker sends a notice to a separate receiver and then marks the stored job done. These are separate operations; there is no transaction spanning them.
A worker may stop at any point, and an old worker may continue running after its lease expires.
A send request may time out even if the receiver accepted it. The sender cannot infer acceptance from a timeout.
In the current design the receiver does not deduplicate requests.
We do not yet know whether the receiver can be changed to support durable idempotency keys.
Jobs can be retried. Eventual delivery requires that retries continue and some attempt eventually succeeds.
For this project a missed notice is worse than a duplicate, but duplicates should be prevented where the rules allow.
